description: We’re a team of Electrical Engineering students interested in software development, electronics, data analysis, and real-world applications of technology. For NASA Space Apps, our goal of turning complex satellite data into something useful, intuitive, and accessible. We enjoy building things from the ground up and combining different technical perspectives to solve challenging problems.
summary:
REDZONE is a web app that turns NASA satellite fire data into clear, everyday answers. Our question: Before you plan a day outside, how do you know whether it is safe from fire? REDZONE answers with three things: where fires burned over the past year, how risky the next 7 days look, and whether fire has been detected near a place or event you care about.

We merged 21.2 million NASA FIRMS fire detections from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors (Nov 2025 to Nov 2026) into one checked database, flagging doubtful records instead of deleting any. Our statistical test showed that fire power cannot be reliably converted between the two sensors, so REDZONE always reports them separately. On top of the data we built an interactive fire map, place search, live statistics, a 7-day fire-risk outlook based on the Fosberg Fire Weather Index, event checks, priority sites and email alerts, with new NASA data added every 3 hours.

Raw satellite data is powerful but hard for ordinary people to use. REDZONE makes it reliable and easy to read.
details:
What it does and how it works

REDZONE combines one year of NASA FIRMS active-fire data (1 Nov 2025 to 1 Nov 2026) from two sensors: MODIS on Terra and Aqua (about 1 km pixels, 3,386,208 detections) and VIIRS on NOAA-21 (375 m pixels, 17,780,994 detections). That is 21,167,202 detections in total.

Data preparation: eight scripted steps turned the raw FIRMS files into one 446 MB DuckDB database. We standardized the files, audited all 87 file layouts, put both sensors into one shared layout with a sensor label on every row, checked for duplicates (none found), and validated coordinates, dates, times, and confidence values. No record was deleted. Problem values (8 negative and 7,922 zero fire-power values, plus 391 polar detections) are flagged instead. The largest polar cluster, 307 detections on 110 days, turned out to be Mount Erebus, an active volcano in Antarctica. NASA's original values are never overwritten; every derived value goes in a new column.

Calibration: MODIS confidence (0–100) was mapped onto VIIRS's low/nominal/high scale using NASA's published classes, so both sensors can be filtered together. We also tested whether fire radiative power (FRP) could be converted between the sensors. We used 894 grid cells where both satellites passed within 10 minutes and compared five methods (no conversion, constant ratio, OLS, RMA, and Deming regression) on held-out weeks. None beat "no conversion"; per-cell differences reached about a factor of 3. So REDZONE always shows each sensor's fire power separately and never adds them together.

The web app:

- Fire map: a heat grid when zoomed out and every individual detection when zoomed in. Click a detection for its sensor, time, confidence, FRP, and coordinates. Dark, satellite, and street basemaps are available.

- Filters: time period, sensor, confidence.

- Search and "Near me": find any place or coordinates, or use your own location to count fires within 10–100 km.

- Live statistics: detection counts, FRP per sensor, a day/night split, and a daily chart for whatever is on the map.

- 7-day fire-risk outlook: the Open-Meteo forecast is converted into the Fosberg Fire Weather Index. The level drops one step when 2 mm or more of rain is forecast and rises one step for areas with a fire-prone local history.

- Event checks: save an event (name, date, place, radius). 12 hours before it starts, REDZONE checks for nearby fires and the fire weather during the event.

- Priority sites and email alerts: mark places to protect, such as a data centre, and get alerts when new moderate- or high-confidence fires appear inside the radius.

- Live updates: every 3 hours, new NASA near-real-time data is downloaded and run through the same cleaning rules as the historical data.

Benefits and intended impact

REDZONE turns a large, technical dataset into answers a normal person can act on: is there fire near me, near my event, or near a place I care about, and how risky is this week? It helps people planning outdoor activities, and organisations watching critical sites, to see fire activity early. It also shows how open NASA data can be made reliable and easy to use without hiding its limits.

Tools and technologies

Python, pandas, PyArrow, DuckDB, FastAPI and Uvicorn (backend); Leaflet and Chart.js with HTML/CSS/JavaScript (frontend); matplotlib (analysis). Data and services: NASA FIRMS archive and area API, Open-Meteo weather forecasts, and OpenStreetMap search (Photon and Nominatim).

How it is creative

Instead of just plotting fire points, REDZONE starts from an everyday question, "Is my picnic safe from fire?", and combines past detections, live data, and weather into one answer. The event check runs automatically before your plans.

Factors our team considered

- Data integrity: no deletions, original values preserved, every cleaning decision reviewable.

- Sensor differences: different pixel sizes mean detection counts and fire power are not directly comparable, so they are kept separate.

- Honest limits: satellites pass only a few times a day and can miss fires under clouds or smoke; the outlook ignores vegetation and drought; near-real-time data has no fire-type field. The site shows these limits.

- Avoiding alert fatigue: alerts include only moderate- or high-confidence fires above a fire-power threshold the user chooses.

- Privacy: device location is used only with permission; otherwise an approximate, clearly labelled IP location is used.

- Performance and reliability: the map loads only the visible area (at most 20,000 points), and switches basemap automatically if a provider fails.

- Safety: REDZONE is a research prototype, not an official warning service. Users are always told to follow local authorities.
